The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

derivations.claim: Choose a bicollar of $T_K$ in $S^3$ and thicken $E_K$ and $N(K)$ slightly to an open cover. The two sets deformation-retract to $E_K$ and $N(K)$, and their intersection deformation-retracts to $T_K$. By [F1] and [F2], the segment $H_2(S^3;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\oplus H_1(N(K);\mathbb Z)\to H_1(S^3;\mathbb Z)$ has zero groups at both ends, so the middle map is an isomorphism.

Let $M=E_K(p/q)$ and choose a bicollar of the gluing torus. Thickening the exterior and attached solid torus across this collar gives an open cover of $M$ whose two sets retract to the pieces and whose intersection retracts to $T_K$. Write $\alpha=p\mu+q\lambda$, and choose $\beta=r\mu+s\lambda$ with $ps-qr=1$, so $\alpha,\beta$ form a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$. In the Mayer–Vietoris map, $\alpha$ maps to $(p[\mu],0)$ because it bounds the attached solid-torus meridian disk, and $\beta$ maps to $(r[\mu],\pm v)$ where $v$ generates the first homology of the attached solid torus; the coefficient is $\pm1$ because $\beta$ intersects $\alpha$ once. The pieces and their overlap are path-connected: the exterior is a connected manifold and hence path-connected, and the solid torus and boundary torus are path-connected. By [F6], the following $H_0$ map sends $1$ to $(1,-1)$ and is injective. Exactness therefore identifies $H_1(M;\mathbb Z)$ with the cokernel of the $H_1$ map.

By [F3], $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^2$, and by [F4] and [F2] the solid torus $N(K)\simeq S^1$ has $H_1(N(K);\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$. Since $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\oplus\mathbb Z\cong\mathbb Z^2$, the direct summand $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is free of rank one. Under the isomorphism in step 1.1, $\mu$ maps to $([\mu],0)$ because it bounds a disk in $N(K)$. The longitude maps to $(0,\pm1)$: [A1] gives its zero exterior image, and degree $+1$ on the core gives a generator of $H_1(N(K);\mathbb Z)$ under the deformation-retraction identification. Since the map is an isomorphism, $[\mu]$ generates $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$.

Thus $H_1(M;\mathbb Z)$ has generators $[\mu],v$ and relations $p[\mu]=0$ and $r[\mu]\pm v=0$. Eliminating $v$ leaves $\mathbb Z\langle[\mu]\rangle/\langle p[\mu]\rangle$. If $p\ne0$, this is $\mathbb Z/|p|\mathbb Z$; if $p=0$, coprimality gives $q=\pm1$ and the group is $\mathbb Z$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the base configuration of
[[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]], with $h=\frac{1}{4(n+1)}$ and
$q_j=((2j-n-1)h,0)$. Fix an index $i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$. The two adjacent
base points are

$$q_i=\bigl((2i-n-1)h,0\bigr),\qquad q_{i+1}=\bigl((2i+1-n)h,0\bigr),$$

their **midpoint** is $m_i:=(q_i+q_{i+1})/2=((2i-n)h,0)=q_i+(h,0)$, and their
**support disc** is the open disc

$$U_i:=\bigl\{w\in\mathbb R^2:\lVert w-m_i\rVert_2<\tfrac32h\bigr\}.$$

The support disc contains the two base points $q_i,q_{i+1}$, whose distance from
$m_i$ is $h$, and it contains no other base point: for $k<i$ one has
$\lVert q_k-m_i\rVert_2=(2(i-k)+1)h\ge 3h$ and for $k>i+1$ one has
$\lVert q_k-m_i\rVert_2=(2(k-i)-1)h\ge3h$, both exceeding $\tfrac32h$. Moreover
$U_i\subseteq D^\circ$, because every point of $U_i$ has norm at most
$\lVert m_i\rVert_2+\tfrac32h\le(n-2)h+\tfrac32h<(n+1)h<1$. Finally
$U_i\cap U_j=\varnothing$ whenever $|i-j|>1$, since then the midpoints are at
distance $2|i-j|h\ge4h>3h$, twice the radius.

**The positive half twist.** Define $\rho\colon I\to\mathbb R^2$, the
**anticlockwise diamond path**, by

$$\rho(t):=\begin{cases}\bigl(2th-h,\,-2th\bigr),&0\le t\le \tfrac12,\\[2pt] \bigl(2th-h,\,2th-2h\bigr),&\tfrac12\le t\le1.\end{cases}$$

Thus $\rho(0)=(-h,0)$, $\rho(\tfrac12)=(0,-h)$, $\rho(1)=(h,0)$, and $\rho$ is
continuous, piecewise linear, and satisfies $\lVert\rho(t)\rVert_2\le h$ for all
$t$ with $\rho(t)\neq0$ throughout. The **elementary half twist at $i$**, written
$\sigma_i$, is the tuple of motions

$$(\sigma_i)_i(t):=m_i+\rho(t),\qquad (\sigma_i)_{i+1}(t):=m_i-\rho(t),\qquad (\sigma_i)_k(t):=q_k\ \ (k\notin\{i,i+1\}).$$

It is a braid based at $Q$
([[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]],
[[def-continuous-map-top]]): the two moving points stay in $U_i$ and are
antipodal about $m_i$, so they are distinct; every other point is fixed and lies
outside $U_i$; and the endpoint permutation is the transposition of $i$ and
$i+1$, since $(\sigma_i)_i(1)=m_i+(h,0)=q_{i+1}$ and
$(\sigma_i)_{i+1}(1)=m_i-(h,0)=q_i$.

The words *positive* and *anticlockwise* refer to the fixed orientation of the
plane of the disc and to the fixed planar projection whose horizontal axis
contains $Q$: the moving pair turns through the half turn anticlockwise, the
label $i$ passing below its midpoint and the label $i+1$ above. Together with
the first-under-second stacking convention of
[[prop-stacking-of-geometric-braids-is-well-defined]] this fixes the sign
convention for every signed crossing on this page and its companion.

**The opposite half twist.** The **opposite** (clockwise) half twist at $i$ is
defined by the reflected path

$$\rho^{-}(t):=\bigl(\rho_1(t),-\rho_2(t)\bigr),$$

through the motions $(\sigma_i^{-})_i(t):=m_i+\rho^{-}(t)$,
$(\sigma_i^{-})_{i+1}(t):=m_i-\rho^{-}(t)$ and
$(\sigma_i^{-})_k(t):=q_k$ for $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$. It is again a braid supported
in $U_i$ with endpoint permutation the transposition of $i$ and $i+1$; its pair
turns through the same half turn clockwise, the label $i$ passing above the
midpoint. The two motions are not equal, and they are not related by a
reparametrisation of the height: they are the two signed crossings of the pair.

**The opposite motion is the group inverse.** For a braid $\beta$ the reversed
braid $\overline\beta_j(t)=z_{\pi(\beta)^{-1}(j)}(1-t)$ represents
$[\beta]^{-1}$ in the group $G_n$
([[thm-geometric-braids-form-a-group]]). For $\beta=\sigma_i$ one computes
$\overline{\sigma_i}=\sigma_i^{-}$: reversing the height and relabelling by the
transposition of $i$ and $i+1$ sends $\rho(t)=m_i+(\rho_1,\rho_2)$ to the
motion with relative path $-\rho(1-t)$, which is the reflected path
$\rho^-$ traversed from $t=0$ to $t=1$. Hence

$$[\sigma_i^{-}]=[\sigma_i]^{-1}\qquad\text{in }G_n .$$

**Elementary cases.** For $n\le1$ there is no index $i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$,
and there are no elementary half twists; the assertions above are vacuous. For
$n\ge2$ and $1\le i\le n-1$ both $[\sigma_i]$ and $[\sigma_i^{-}]$ are
nonidentity elements of $G_n$, since their endpoint permutations are
transpositions, which are not the identity permutation.

**Two letters do not commute in general.** For adjacent indices the supports
$U_i$ and $U_{i+1}$ overlap and no commutation is asserted;
[[lem-geometric-far-commutativity]] proves commutativity only for disjoint
supports.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the base configuration of
[[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]], with $h:=\frac{1}{4(n+1)}$ and
$q_j=((2j-n-1)h,0)$. Let $\beta=(z_1,\dots,z_n)$ and $\gamma=(w_1,\dots,w_n)$
be braids based at $Q$ with endpoint permutations $\pi(\beta)$ and $\pi(\gamma)$
([[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]]), and let $\sim$ denote braid
isotopy relative to the top and bottom
([[def-braid-isotopy-relative-top-and-bottom]]).

**(a) The stacked tuple is a braid.** Define $\gamma\star\beta$ by

$$(\gamma\star\beta)_j(t):=\begin{cases}z_j(2t),&0\le t\le\tfrac12,\\[2pt] w_{\pi(\beta)(j)}(2t-1),&\tfrac12\le t\le1.\end{cases}$$

Then $\gamma\star\beta$ is a braid based at $Q$. It is the stacking of $\beta$
below $\gamma$: the motion $\beta$ runs during the first half of the height
interval and the motion $\gamma$ during the second half, after the strand of
label $\pi(\beta)(j)$ has been joined.

**(b) The endpoint permutation multiplies.** $\pi(\gamma\star\beta)
=\pi(\gamma)\circ\pi(\beta)$, with $(\pi\circ\sigma)(j)=\pi(\sigma(j))$.

**(c) The operation descends to isotopy classes.** If $\beta\sim\beta'$ and
$\gamma\sim\gamma'$ then $\gamma\star\beta\sim\gamma'\star\beta'$.

**(d) The operation is associative.** If $\delta$ is a further braid based at
$Q$, then $(\delta\star\gamma)\star\beta\sim\delta\star(\gamma\star\beta)$.

**(e) The endpoint permutation is constant along isotopies.** If
$\beta\sim\beta'$ then $\pi(\beta)=\pi(\beta')$; equivalently $\pi$ is constant
on each braid isotopy class, so that $\pi$ is a function of the class $[\beta]$
alone.

Consequently the stacking of isotopy classes,
$[\gamma]\,[\beta]:=[\gamma\star\beta]$, is a well-defined associative binary
operation on the set of braid isotopy classes based at $Q$, with
$\pi(\delta\star\gamma\star\beta)=\pi(\delta)\pi(\gamma)\pi(\beta)$ for any
three braids.

Let $n\ge0$ and let $\beta=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$ be a geometric braid with
the fixed real basepoints $q_j=((2j-n-1)/(4(n+1)),0)$ and endpoint
permutation $\pi$, as in [[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]].
Identify the disk with $\{x\in\mathbb C:|x|<1\}$ and put
$$V=(D^\circ\times[0,1])/((x,1)\sim(x,0)).$$
The quotient and its topology use [[def-product-topology]] and the circle
$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ of [[def-circle-as-real-line-mod-integers]].
The interval images
$$s_j=\{[(z_j(t),t)]:0\le t\le1\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(\beta)=\bigcup_{j=1}^n s_j$$
are the **closure in the open solid torus**. In general an individual
$s_j$ is an interval image, not a closed circle: its last point is the
first point of $s_{\pi(j)}$.

**Components and orientation.** For a cycle
$(j,\pi(j),\ldots,\pi^{k-1}(j))$ concatenate these $k$ strand maps in
that order, with parameter in $[0,k]$. Their endpoints agree in $V$,
so the concatenation factors through $\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$.
It is injective on this circle: points at distinct nonintegral heights
can agree only when their parameters have the same fractional part,
and the distinct strands at that height have distinct disk coordinates;
at integral heights only the specified adjacent endpoints agree.
Thus each cycle gives an embedded circle. Different cycles give
disjoint circles, and every strand belongs to exactly one cycle.
These circles are precisely the connected components of the closure.
The orientation is increasing concatenation parameter. In particular
the number of components equals the number of cycles of $\pi$.

**The standard axis and fixed framing.** In
$S^3=\{(z,w)\in\mathbb C^2:|z|^2+|w|^2=1\}$, as in
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], set
$$A=\{(0,w):|w|=1\},\qquad P_\theta=\{(z,w)\in S^3:z\ne0,\ \arg z=\theta\}.$$
Fix the following particular diffeomorphism, including its disk framing:
$$\varphi([(x,t)])=  \bigl(\sqrt{1-|x|^2}\,e^{2\pi it},x\bigr):  V\longrightarrow S^3\setminus A.$$
Its inverse has disk coordinate $x=w$ and circle coordinate
$[t]=[\arg z/(2\pi)]$. Every $P_\theta$ is consequently an open disk.
The **raw topological oriented closure** is
$$\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{top}}=\varphi(\operatorname{cl}(\beta)).$$
This explicit $\varphi$ is part of the construction; the definition
does not allow an arbitrary page-preserving change of framing.

**Page intersections and smooth representatives.** The whole closure
meets every page in exactly $n$ points. A component belonging to a
$\pi$-cycle of length $k$ meets each page in exactly $k$ points:
at any fractional height it uses exactly those $k$ distinct strands.
The page coordinate of its concatenation is $[t]$, for
$t\in\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$, so its oriented degree is $+k$.
If all disk-coordinate strand maps are smooth and have all positive-order derivatives
zero at their endpoints, their cycle concatenations have matching jets
at every seam. The page coordinate has nonzero derivative, so the
result is a smooth embedding of disjoint oriented circles, in the
sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. For an endpoint-flat smooth braid, its literal $\varphi$-image is therefore a smooth oriented link and is denoted $\widehat\beta$.

**Closure in the smooth oriented-link category.** The raw image need not be smooth, even if individual strands are smooth but their endpoint jets fail to match at the cycle seams. For an arbitrary continuous braid, assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) and choose a smooth representative $\beta_s$ by [[lem-every-geometric-braid-is-braid-isotopic-to-a-smooth-braid]]. Make it endpoint-flat by composing all disk-coordinate strands with a fixed smooth nondecreasing $\psi:I\to I$, equal to $0$ near $0$ and $1$ near $1$. Interpolation of height maps $(1-u)t+u\psi(t)$ is an endpoint-fixed braid isotopy, because every strand is evaluated at the same height. The smooth-category closure of $\beta$ is the oriented-link isotopy class of this chosen model's literal $\varphi$-image; when a subset is needed, use that chosen closed-braid representative. Independence of the representative is proved by [[lem-closure-depends-only-on-the-braid-isotopy-class]]. Page and cycle properties refer to the chosen constructed closed braid, with the same number of strands and endpoint permutation as $\beta$.

If $\beta$ already has smooth strands with matching cycle-seam jets, in particular if it is endpoint-flat, its literal raw image is a smooth link and is retained as $\widehat\beta$. The raw quotient, fixed $\varphi$, finite cycles, page counts and trivial closures remain choice-free. Finite elementary words have explicit smooth endpoint-flat models, so forming their literal closures also requires no choice assumption; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used for the general continuous-representative convention and its independence theorem.

**The trivial closure.** For the constant braid its circles are
$\{(\sqrt{1-q_j^2}e^{2\pi it},q_j):[t]\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\}$.
They are latitudes of the sphere
$S=\{(z,w)\in S^3:\operatorname{Im}w=0\}$, with
$\operatorname{Re}w=q_j$. Each northern cap
$C_j=\{p\in S:\operatorname{Re}w(p)\ge q_j\}$ is a smooth disk:
stereographic coordinates on $S$ give radius
$\sqrt{(1-q_j)/(1+q_j)}$ for this cap. To make their spanning disks
disjoint, let $e$ be the unit vector in the $\operatorname{Im}w$
direction, set $\varepsilon=\pi/16$ and
$f_j(p)=\varepsilon(\operatorname{Re}w(p)-q_j)$ on $C_j$, and use
$$F_j(p)=\cos(f_j(p))p+\sin(f_j(p))e.$$
The boundary is fixed. The tubular parametrization
$(p,s)\mapsto\cos(s)p+\sin(s)e$ is injective for $|s|<\pi/2$,
and $0\le f_j<\pi/8$. On overlapping caps, if $q_i<q_j$ then
$f_i-f_j=\varepsilon(q_j-q_i)>0$, so their graphs are disjoint.
Thus these are pairwise disjoint smooth spanning disks. The trivial
$n$-braid closes to the oriented $n$-component unlink; for $n=1$
this is the unknot.

At $n=0$ all strand and cycle unions are empty, every page has zero intersections,
and the closure is the empty link. The basepoint list and disk constructions
above then have no entries.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the smooth normal-bundle structure used in the
framing clause. For a knot component $K$, its normal bundle is the fibrewise
quotient $\nu K=TS^3|_K/TK$, and a normal section is a smooth section of this
bundle.

Let $D$ be a regular oriented link diagram in a projection plane $P$ of an
oriented $3$-sphere, after moving the link off the point at infinity. Fix the
unit viewing normal $n$ pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ by the rule that
an ordered basis $(u,v)$ of $P$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is a positive
basis of the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, let $v_{\rm over}$ and
$v_{\rm under}$ be the nonzero projected tangent vectors following the
orientations of the overpassing and underpassing strands. Define
$$\operatorname{sgn}(c):=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})\in\{+1,-1\}.$$
Reversing the orientation of $P$ reverses every crossing sign.

This convention makes the positive geometric Artin half twist positive. In
the braid chart $(x,y,t)$ with ambient orientation $(x,y,t)$, view along $+y$;
the induced positive orientation of the $(x,t)$ projection plane is the ordered
basis $(\partial_t,\partial_x)$. For the positive half twist, label $i$ moves
from $x=-h$ to $x=h$ below the midpoint, while label $i+1$ moves from $x=h$ to
$x=-h$ above it, with $h>0$. Thus the over and under projected tangent vectors
in coordinates $(t,x)$ are $(1,-2h)$ and $(1,2h)$, whose determinant is
$4h>0$.

The **writhe** of $D$ is
$$\operatorname{wr}(D):=\sum_{c\text{ a crossing of }D}\operatorname{sgn}(c).$$
For a link component $K_i$, its **self-writhe**
$\operatorname{wr}_i(D)$ is the sum over crossings whose two branches belong to
$K_i$; the total writhe also includes all mixed crossings between distinct
components.

The **blackboard framing** of a component of $D$ is the homotopy class of the
normal section represented by the positive quarter-turn in $P$ of the projected
oriented tangent. The projection is an immersion, so this vector never
vanishes; it is perpendicular to the projected tangent, hence also to the
spatial tangent, and therefore represents a nonzero normal section of the
component in the ambient $3$-sphere.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8,>=stealth]
  \draw[->] (-1,0) -- (1,0) node[right] {$v_{\rm over}$};
  \draw[->] (0,-1) -- (0,1) node[above] {$v_{\rm under}$};
  \node[above left] at (0,0) {$+1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

In the displayed local chart, the over tangent is the positive horizontal
vector and the under tangent is the positive vertical vector, so the determinant
is $+1$. This figure illustrates the determinant rule only; no proof below
depends on a picture.

Orient the projection plane by the viewing normal and the ambient orientation. At an oriented crossing let $o$ be the over-arc, and let $n_o$ be its positive in-plane normal: the ordered pair consisting of the over-tangent and $n_o$ is positive. Call the under-side from which $n_o$ points the source $s$, and the side toward which it points the target $t$. A positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk whose orientation, preceded by the oriented knot tangent, is the ambient orientation. With the common upper-collar basing paths, the based positive meridians satisfy
$$m_t=m_o^{-1}m_s m_o.$$
This side-based equation is independent of the direction of the understrand. In an oriented chart with over-tangent rightward, the target is the upper side $L$ and source the lower side $R$, so equivalently $m_R=m_o m_Lm_o^{-1}$. In incoming/outgoing notation, the outgoing under-meridian is $m_o^{-1}m_{\rm in}m_o$ if the under-tangent points along $n_o$, and is $m_om_{\rm in}m_o^{-1}$ otherwise. Reversing a chosen meridian loop inverts its class. Changing every common access path by the same based loop conjugates all three classes simultaneously.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $D$ be a valid finite planar code for a regular diagram of $K$, choose a basepoint $b$ in the complement, and designate a starting under-arc. The finite procedure $\mathsf{Wirtinger}(D,a_0)$ terminates and returns a presentation with one positive-meridian generator for each under-arc and one crossing conjugacy relator for each crossing. For the based meridians determined by the diagram's common upper-collar paths from $b$, the homomorphism from the presented group to $\pi_1(S^3\setminus K,b)$ that sends each generator to its corresponding based positive meridian is an isomorphism. Changing the designated starting under-arc only relabels the same finite cyclic arc set and gives an isomorphic presentation. If all basing paths are changed by prepending the same based loop, every generator image is conjugated by the same element, so the isomorphism type is unchanged.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a regular oriented diagram
of a knot $K$ with blackboard framing $b_D$. The self-linking number of the
framed knot $(K,b_D)$ equals the diagram writhe:
$$\operatorname{sl}(K,b_D)=\operatorname{wr}(D).$$
More generally, let $D$ be a regular oriented diagram of an oriented link
$L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r$, and let $b_{D,i}$ be the blackboard framing
of $K_i$ induced by its component subdiagram. Then
$\operatorname{sl}(K_i,b_{D,i})=\operatorname{wr}_i(D)\qquad(1\le i\le r).$ Total writhe of a link still includes
the signs of mixed crossings, while the sum of component self-linking numbers
uses only self-crossings.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For an oriented smooth knot
$K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$, its normal bundle is
$\nu K=TS^3|_K/TK$, oriented so that a positive tangent to $K$ followed by a
positive basis of a normal fibre gives the ambient orientation. A **framing**
of $K$ is a homotopy class through smooth nowhere-zero sections of $\nu K$.
The normal bundle is made a smooth vector bundle under this axiom; a framed
knot includes the section class as data, not a choice made afterwards. For the
relative integer use the round metric transferred from the unit sphere in
$\mathbb R^4$ by the explicit diffeomorphism
$$x\longmapsto\left(\frac{2x}{1+\lVert x\rVert^2},\frac{\lVert x\rVert^2-1}{1+\lVert x\rVert^2}\right),\qquad\infty\longmapsto(0,0,0,1).$$
It induces a smooth bundle metric on $\nu K$. The resulting winding number is
independent of the metric: any two smooth fibre metrics interpolate through
positive metrics and the corresponding angle maps are homotopic.

Given a reference framing $[s_0]$ and another framing $[s_1]$, use a bundle
metric and the positive quarter-turn $J$ on each oriented normal plane. Choose
representatives $s_0,s_1$ and normalize both to unit sections
$\widehat s_i(x):=s_i(x)/\lVert s_i(x)\rVert$. Write
$$\widehat s_1(x)=\cos\theta(x)\widehat s_0(x)+\sin\theta(x)J\widehat s_0(x).$$
The resulting map $S^1\to S^1$ has a continuous angle lift along a parameter
interval $[0,1]$: subdivide into finitely many intervals whose images lie in
open semicircles and choose consecutive local arguments agreeing at endpoints.
Since the map is closed, the lift satisfies $\theta(1)-\theta(0)=2\pi m$ for
some $m\in\mathbb Z$; different lifts differ by a constant multiple of
$2\pi$, and homotopies keep $m$ fixed. Conversely, the difference between
$\theta(t)$ and $\theta(0)+2\pi mt$ is periodic, so linear interpolation of
these angles gives a homotopy to the degree-$m$ rotation of $\widehat s_0$.
Every integer occurs by such a rotation. Thus $m$ classifies the framing class
relative to $[s_0]$ and gives the **relative framing integer**. Once a reference
framing is supplied, the framing classes are an integer torsor; no absolute
integer is assigned before choosing a reference.

The **self-linking number** of a framed knot $(K,[s])$ is the linking number
of $K$ with a sufficiently small push-off along $s$, oriented parallel to $K$.
The push-off and its integer are independent of the representative section,
small radius, and normalized tubular chart by the preceding well-definedness
result.

If a compact oriented surface $\Sigma$ is supplied with boundary $K$, its
**Seifert framing relative to $\Sigma$** is the homotopy class of the inward
unit conormal to $K$ in $\Sigma$, viewed as a nonzero normal section to $K$ in
$S^3$. This definition is relative to the supplied surface; it neither asserts
that every knot bounds such a surface nor asserts the self-linking-zero result.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

For every path-connected topological space $X$ and $x_0\in X$, the Hurewicz map
$$h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
is surjective and has kernel $[\pi_1(X,x_0),\pi_1(X,x_0)]$. Hence it induces a natural isomorphism
$$\pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X;\mathbb Z).$$
The proof is choice-free and requires no CW, separation, local path-connectivity or local simple-connectivity assumption.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented $3$-sphere, let $N(K)$ be a chosen closed tubular solid-torus neighborhood, let $E_K=\overline{S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)}$, and let $T_K=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$. Let $\mu$ be the positive oriented meridian, meaning the boundary of a positive normal disk in $N(K)$, and let $\lambda$ be a preferred longitude, meaning a degree-one parallel of the core $K$ in $N(K)$ that is null-homologous in $E_K$. Assume that $[\mu],[\lambda]$ are an ordered basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$, with the boundary-orientation convention $\mu\cdot\lambda=-1$. A slope is the unoriented isotopy class of an essential simple closed curve on $T_K$ whose homology class is $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ for coprime integers $p,q$ not both zero; $(p,q)$ and $(-p,-q)$ represent the same slope. For a slope represented by $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$, the Dehn filling $E_K(p/q)$ is obtained by gluing an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to $E_K$ by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{1\}]$ to that slope; the filled orientation agrees with the fixed orientation on $E_K$. If $q\ne0$, the coefficient is written $p/q$; the meridional slope is $1/0$, and integer $n$-framed filling means slope $n[\mu]+[\lambda]$. The oriented homeomorphism type is independent of the gluing map once its meridian image is fixed.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Work with smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere; a knot is a one-component oriented link. A **finite planar code for an oriented knot diagram** consists of finite vertex and edge sets, incidence data, a cyclic order of the four half-edges at every crossing vertex, a pairing of opposite half-edges into the two local branches, an orientation of each edge, and a choice of which branch is over at each crossing. Every other vertex is a bend vertex of valence two. The code includes a finite plane-drawing certificate: rational coordinates for the vertices and bends, and a finite polygonal path for every edge. The certificate must realize the incidences and cyclic orders, have no edge self-intersection, and have pairwise disjoint edge interiors except at the specified bend and crossing vertices; at a crossing the two branches must be transverse. These conditions are checked by finitely many exact segment-intersection tests. Edge orientations must join coherently across each paired branch and each bend vertex, and following the edges through the crossing pairings and the degree-two bend vertices must give one oriented circle. Thus an admissible code represents a connected regular oriented diagram of a single knot. If there are no crossing vertices, the code is one oriented polygonal circle and has one arc. Smooth each bend in a small disk disjoint from all crossings and other edges; the resulting smooth diagram has the same crossing data.

An **under-arc** is a maximal portion of the oriented circle between consecutive points where the knot passes under at a crossing; the over branch is not cut. With no crossings the entire circle is the unique under-arc. A **positive meridian** of an oriented branch is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk, with disk orientation chosen so that the oriented tangent to the branch followed by the disk orientation agrees with the ambient orientation of $S^3$. Planarity, incidence, orientation consistency, one-component tracing and the over/under data are input validity conditions; a procedure receiving an invalid finite record must report invalid input rather than repair it. The code stores no algebraic crossing sign: the oriented plane and the direction of the over branch determine which incident under branch is on its left and which is on its right.

derivations.claim: In [F1], for $0<t<1/2$ the left-starting motion is $(2ht-h,-2ht)$ and the right-starting motion its negative. At the crossing the latter has greater $y$, hence is over when viewed along $+y$. Their projected tangents in coordinates $(t,x)$ are $(1,-2h)$ and $(1,2h)$, with determinant $4h>0$. Rounding the diamond corners and flattening endpoints preserves this strict sign. The downward three-crossing diagram therefore has three positive crossings. The diagram agrees with the fixed geometric closure: the change from stacked diamonds to rounded diagonal strands is a height-preserving interpolation with nonzero pair difference, followed by the fixed closure map. In particular it is not the mirror braid.

Label the initial left and right meridians $a,b$. At a positive crossing the right input is over, and the left input follows the positive over-normal to become the right output. Successive rows of the braid have input/output pairs $\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}\text{row}&\text{input }(L,R)&\text{output }(L,R)&\text{underpass relation}\\\hline1&(a,b)&(b,c)&c=b^{-1}ab\\2&(b,c)&(c,a)&a=c^{-1}bc\\3&(c,a)&(a,b)&b=a^{-1}ca\end{array}$ Here the last two output labels use the closure identifications of bottom and top positions. By [F8], this is the finite three-crossing code to which the Wirtinger correctness theorem [F3] applies. These are all crossing relations by [F3]. Substituting $c=b^{-1}ab$ into $b=a^{-1}ca$ gives $aba=bab$; the remaining relation follows because $b^{-1}ab=aba^{-1}$ and then $c^{-1}bc=a$. Thus $\pi_1(S^3\setminus T)=\langle a,b\mid aba=bab\rangle$, with the stated positive meridians. In the chosen tube, the radial normal homotopy from positive radius $r<\epsilon$ to $(1-s)r+s\epsilon$ identifies this group with $\pi_1(E_T)$.

Trace a small parallel starting at the initial left arc. Along the oriented component its underpasses occur in row order $1,3,2$, with over-meridians $b,a,c$; it passes over the intervening crossings. This order follows directly from the input/output table: $a$ becomes $c$ on the right in row 1, passes over in row 2, becomes $b$ in row 3, closes to the initial right position, passes over in row 1, becomes $a$ in row 2 and closes after passing over in row 3. At each underpass the access-path calculation in [F3] is $\alpha_{\rm in}\beta=g_o\alpha_{\rm out}$, where $\beta$ is the path along the small parallel; thus the three successive factors are $b,a,c$, with positive exponents. At an overpass the access path slides through its upper product chart and contributes no factor. On the crossing-free exterior closure arcs use the same product charts, again contributing no factor. Concatenating gives the based parallel word $w=bac$. These path identities can be made on the upper side of the normal circles. The upper normal section and the blackboard section are homotopic without zero: in the normal quotient the blackboard vector and viewing vector form a positively oriented basis, so the interpolation rotating the former through a fixed quarter-turn to the latter is everywhere nonzero. This proves that the traced parallel has the blackboard framing and oriented degree $+1$, rather than identifying a peripheral word only from its exponent sum. By [F4] and step 1.1 its self-linking is $+3$.

The boundary torus has product coordinates from this actual parallel: its degree-one section is $w$ and its positive fibre is $a$. A section making three negative fibre turns is an embedded degree-one curve with based word $w a^{-3}$; the torus rectangle homotopy makes the fibre and section commute. In the abelianization of step 2.1 the relation $aba=bab$ gives $[a]=[b]$, and sending each to $1$ supplies an inverse to the cyclic generator map. Thus $H_1(E_T)=\mathbb Z$ on $[a]$ by [F6], and $[w]=[b]+[a]+[c]=3[a]$. Therefore $\lambda=w a^{-3}$ has zero exterior homology and degree $+1$, precisely [F5]. Moreover $c=aba^{-1}$, so $w a^3=b a^2b a^2=b a(bab)a=(ba)^3=(ab)^3.$ Both last cubes equal $(aba)^2$, which commutes with $a,b$ because conjugation by $aba$ exchanges them. This proves $\lambda=(ab)^3a^{-6}$ with the fixed positive meridian and the correct sign.

The $+1$ slope is the primitive boundary curve $\lambda\mu$, since its coefficients in the oriented meridian/longitude basis are $(1,1)$. In [F7] the solid torus has cyclic fundamental group; a complementary boundary generator identifies its core generator and eliminates it, while its meridian kills precisely $\lambda\mu$. Thus filling adds $w a^{-2}=1$. Substituting $w=bac$ and $c=b^{-1}ab$ gives $bab^{-1}aba^{-2}=1$. Equivalently step 4.1 gives $(ab)^3=a^5$. These are the asserted presentations of the same positive-trefoil $+1$ filling.

citations.quote:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented $3$-sphere, choose a closed tubular neighborhood $N(K)$, and set $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ and $T_K=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$; assume $E_K$ is connected. Let $\mu$ be the oriented boundary of a normal disk whose orientation, preceded by the oriented tangent to $K$, agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. Let $\lambda$ be a simple closed curve on $T_K$ whose degree under the normal-tube projection $T_K\to K$ is $+1$ and whose image in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is zero; such a curve is a preferred longitude. Assume $([\mu],[\lambda])$ is an ordered basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$. For coprime integers $p,q$ not both zero, let $E_K(p/q)$ be the filling whose attached solid-torus meridian maps to $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$. Then
$$H_1(E_K(p/q);\mathbb Z)\cong\begin{cases}\mathbb Z/|p|\mathbb Z,&p\ne0,\\[2pt]\mathbb Z,&p=0.\end{cases}$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented $3$-sphere with a chosen exterior $E_K$ and peripheral basis $(\mu,\lambda)$, where $\lambda$ is preferred. For $n\in\mathbb Z$, attach one smooth $4$-dimensional $2$-handle $D^2\times D^2$ to the $4$-ball $B^4$ along $S^1\times D^2$ in $\partial B^4=S^3$ by the standard orientation-compatible handle attachment, using a product framing whose attaching parallel on $\partial E_K$ has slope $n[\mu]+[\lambda]$.
